papers.title: When Less is More: Investigating Data Pruning for Pretraining LLMs at Scale
papers.pitch: Training on just 30% of web-scraped pretraining data can outperform using the entire dataset—if you keep the “medium-quality” examples, not the best or worst. Surprisingly, simple perplexity ranking beats more expensive quality metrics for this data pruning, overturning beliefs that harder data is always better.

papers.title: M3DSYNTH: A DATASET OF MEDICAL 3D IMAGES WITH AI-GENERATED LOCAL MANIPULATIONS
papers.pitch: AI-injected or removed lung cancer nodules in CT scans easily fool automated diagnostic tools and even human experts, yet detectors trained on natural images fail on medical data. Our M3Dsynth dataset enables forensic detectors to accurately localize these synthetic manipulations and generalize across unseen generator types—but only when fine-tuned on medical scans.

papers.title: What's In My Big Data?
papers.pitch: Nearly 50% of documents in RedPajama and LAION-2B-en are exact duplicates, while benchmark contamination is rampant—over 64% of Winograd Schema Challenge instances appear in widely used training corpora. WIMBD provides scalable search and count primitives to systematically uncover these hidden failures in the datasets powering today’s language models.

Rephrasing the Web: A Recipe for Compute and Data-Efficient Language
  Modeling

This works because the synthetic text is both cleaner and stylistically closer to how we actually query models, even though it adds no new facts.

papers.title: MetaEmbed: Scaling Multimodal Retrieval at Test-Time with Flexible Late Interaction
papers.pitch: Current multimodal retrieval forces an impossible choice between fast but information-poor single-vector models and accurate but prohibitively expensive multi-vector methods. papers.title: Video models are zero-shot learners and reasoners

papers.title: Intern-S1-Pro: Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model at Trillion Scale

papers.title: Generating Sequences With Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.pitch: A recurrent neural network can learn to dream—generating novel Wikipedia articles and strikingly human handwriting simply by guessing the next data point. papers.title: DeepWalk: Online Learning of Social Representations

papers.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
papers.pitch: Byte pair encoding lets neural machine translation handle any word by splitting rare terms into frequent subword pieces—no dictionary backup needed. This single change boosts translation of unseen words from near-zero to usable levels, especially across different alphabets, because the network learns to transliterate and compose words from scratch.

papers.title: Unsupervised Representation Learning with Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks

papers.title: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information
papers.pitch: Word embeddings can now be built for any word, even ones never seen during training, simply by summing vectors for its character n-grams. This simple trick not only generates state-of-the-art representations for rare and morphologically complex words but also achieves performance comparable to a full-data baseline while using only 5% of the training corpus.

papers.title: Prototypical Networks for Few-shot Learning

papers.title: Deep contextualized word representations
papers.pitch: Unlike traditional word vectors that assign each word a single fixed meaning, ELMo represents words as deep, context-dependent functions of entire sentences—dramatically slashing errors by up to 20% across six major NLP tasks simply by plugging into existing models.

papers.title: Contrastive Predictive Coding
papers.pitch: Simply trying to predict the future directly in pixel or audio space has failed for decades — CPC shows that splitting the task into a compact latent encoder plus a contrastive loss that only has to rank plausible continuations against random negatives finally unlocks powerful, universal representations across speech, images, text, and 3D environments.

papers.title: Large Scale GAN Training for High Fidelity Natural Image Synthesis
papers.pitch: Simply scaling up GANs by 2–4x in parameters and 8x in batch size slashes ImageNet generation FID from 18.65 to 7.4, but this brute-force approach surfaces a brutal trade-off: the discriminator inevitably memorizes the training set and the generator's spectral norm spirals toward collapse, forcing you to choose between peak performance and training stability.

papers.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
papers.pitch: Bidirectional pre-training obliterates unidirectional models across 11 NLP benchmarks—BERT sent the GLUE score soaring 7.7 points overnight without any task-specific architecture. The secret? Simply masking random words and forcing the model to guess them from both the left and right context.

papers.title: ERNIE: Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration

papers.title: XLNet: Generalized Autoregressive Pretraining for Language Understanding
papers.pitch: XLNet beats BERT on 20 NLP benchmarks using an autoregressive model—but with a twist: it learns bidirectional context by predicting tokens in random order, not left-to-right. This sidesteps BERT’s reliance on [MASK] tokens and their independence assumption, closing the pretrain-finetune gap while capturing richer dependencies.

papers.title: SpanBERT: Improving Pre-training by Representing and Predicting Spans
papers.pitch: SpanBERT makes a simple but powerful change to BERT's masking: instead of hiding random words, it hides entire spans like "an American football game" and forces the model to predict them using only the boundary words. papers.title: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
papers.pitch: BERT wasn't just undertrained—it was massively so. Simply training the same model longer, on more data, and removing its next-sentence prediction task allows it to match or beat every supposedly superior model that followed, including XLNet. This reveals that many reported architectural gains were actually just training recipe improvements in disguise.

papers.title: DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter
papers.pitch: You can shrink BERT by 40% and it still retains 97% of its language understanding, on condition you teach the small model to mimic the full probability distribution—not just the final answer—of its larger teacher during pre-training.

papers.title: Unsupervised Cross-lingual Representation Learning at Scale

papers.title: PEGASUS: Pre-training with Extracted Gap-sentences for Abstractive Summarization

This Gap Sentences Generation objective enables the model to beat prior work on all 12 tested datasets, and with just 1000 fine-tuning examples it can outperform fully-supervised baselines trained on 100x more data.

papers.title: REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training
papers.pitch: REALM teaches a language model to fetch its own facts from Wikipedia on the fly, learning what to retrieve solely by whether it helps predict missing words—no labeled data needed. This approach outperforms models 30× its size on question answering, proving explicit retrieval can beat implicit memorization.

papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.pitch: A 175B-parameter language model can outperform fine-tuned state-of-the-art systems on NLP benchmarks like TriviaQA and LAMBADA without any weight updates, using only a few demonstrations provided in the prompt. papers.title: Bootstrap Your Own Latent

papers.title: wav2vec 2.0: A Framework for Self-Supervised Learning of Speech Representations
papers.pitch: Jointly learning discrete speech units end‑to‑end lets a model pre‑trained on raw audio reach 4.8/8.2 WER on LibriSpeech using just 10 minutes of labeled data. It surpasses the best semi‑supervised result on the 100‑hour subset while using 100× less labeled data.

papers.pitch: Transformers can extrapolate to sequences twice as long as those seen during training—simply by replacing position embeddings with a linear bias that penalizes attention scores based on token distance. This method even lets a model trained on half the context match the perplexity of a standard model trained on the full length, while training 11% faster.

papers.title: DeBERTaV3: Improving DeBERTa using ELECTRA-Style Pre-Training with Gradient-Disentangled Embedding Sharing
papers.pitch: The shared token embeddings in ELECTRA-based models suffer from a tug-of-war, where the generator pulls similar words together while the discriminator pushes them apart—crashing training efficiency. papers.title: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models

papers.title: UL2: Unifying Language Learning Paradigms
papers.pitch: A single pre-training recipe—mixing span corruption, causal language modeling, and extreme long-span denoising with explicit mode tokens—enables one model to beat both T5 and GPT-style models across the board, including a 20B variant that outperforms 175B GPT-3 on zero-shot SuperGLUE.

papers.title: AudioLM: a Language Modeling Approach to Audio Generation
papers.pitch: A speech generator trained without any text can produce 10-second continuations so coherent that human listeners can’t reliably tell them apart from real recordings. By separately modeling high-level meaning and fine acoustic details with hierarchical language models, the system even preserves an unseen speaker’s voice and prosody across full sentences.

papers.title: RATIONALYST: Mining Implicit Rationales for Process Supervision of Reasoning
papers.pitch: LLMs skip logical steps in chain-of-thought reasoning because their training data is full of unstated premises like 'rule-breaking leads to punishment'—and that omission causes wrong answers. papers.title: Not All LLM Reasoners Are Created Equal
papers.pitch: Most LLMs are much worse at solving chained grade-school math problems than their high benchmark scores suggest, revealing a 'reasoning gap' up to 12× larger in smaller models. This gap stems from distraction and poor multi-hop reasoning—not memorization—proving that near-perfect performance hides systematic brittleness.

papers.title: Inference Scaling for Long-Context Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.pitch: RAG performance scales nearly linearly with compute when you spend it on iterative reasoning and demonstrations, not just more documents—standard RAG plateaus early while their methods achieve up to 58.9% gains.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs through Information Theory
papers.pitch: You can now detect faulty reasoning steps in LLM outputs without any human annotations: each correct step should increase the mutual information with the correct final answer. papers.title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
papers.pitch: Instead of forcing language models to verbalize every reasoning step as words, Coconut feeds the model's own hidden states back as input, creating a “continuous thought.” This allows the model to encode multiple alternative next steps simultaneously—effectively performing an emergent breadth-first search—and significantly outperforms chain-of-thought on logical reasoning that requires backtracking

papers.title: rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking
papers.pitch: A 7B language model achieves 90% on the MATH benchmark without any distillation from larger models by using a self-evolving Monte Carlo Tree Search framework, outperforming OpenAI’s o1-preview. This is enabled by training a step-level process reward model on preference pairs rather than direct scores, avoiding the noise that typically collapses such training. papers.title: Kimi k1.5: Scaling Reinforcement Learning with LLMs
papers.pitch: A plain long-context RL setup—no Monte Carlo tree search, no value functions—matches o1’s reasoning by simply training with 128k-token rollouts. The same long-thinking ability is then compressed into short-CoT models that beat GPT‑4o and Claude Sonnet 3.5 by up to 550% on AIME and LiveCodeBench.

papers.title: s1: Simple test-time scaling
papers.pitch: A model fine-tuned on just 1,000 examples can beat o1-preview on competition math, and simply appending "Wait" during reasoning forces it to double-check and fix its own mistakes—boosting accuracy by up to 7 points without any new training. This paper shows test-time scaling doesn't require large-scale RL or huge datasets, just a tiny curated dataset and a dead-simple forced continuation trick.

papers.title: LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning
papers.pitch: A model fine-tuned on just 817 high-quality examples crushes the AIME math competition (57.1% accuracy), annihilating systems trained on 100× more data and even outperforming OpenAI’s o1-preview. The secret is realizing that modern LLMs already possess the knowledge—they just need a few carefully crafted 'cognitive templates' to unlock it, making massive datasets obsolete for complex reasoning.

papers.title: Gold-medalist Performance in Solving Olympiad Geometry with AlphaGeometry2
papers.pitch: AlphaGeometry2 now outperforms an average IMO gold medalist on geometry, solving 84% of problems from 2000–2024. The breakthrough comes from search trees that share discovered facts in real time, allowing parallel beam searches to collaboratively explore wildly different construction strategies.

papers.title: DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM Reasoning
papers.pitch: DeepSeek-R1’s visible reasoning chains have a performance 'sweet spot': beyond a problem-specific length, more thinking makes accuracy drop—correct thoughts average 40% fewer tokens than incorrect ones. The model also gets trapped in 'rumination', obsessive rechecking of old ideas that blocks progress, and its reasoning mode unlocks jailbreaks that easily compromise safety-aligned models.

papers.title: TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
papers.pitch: A model can bootstrap its own reasoning skills just by practicing on test questions and voting on its answers—no labels needed. papers.title: Llama-Nemotron: Efficient Reasoning Models
papers.pitch: A 253B model outperforms DeepSeek-R1 using NAS-optimized architectures that fit on a single GPU node, delivering even larger reasoning gains on scientific tasks through RL. Remarkably, these are the first open models that let users toggle deep reasoning on and off with a simple system prompt, eliminating the cost of verbose chain-of-thought when it is not needed.

papers.title: REASONING GYM: Reasoning Environments for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.pitch: Training on procedurally generated algorithmic tasks makes a model 29% better at algebra, without ever seeing an algebra problem. papers.title: MiniMax-M1: Scaling Test-Time Compute Efficiently with Lightning Attention

papers.title: RLPR: Extrapolating RLVR to General Domains without Verifiers
papers.pitch: LLMs can be trained to reason better in any domain—without external verifiers—by using their own internal probability of generating the correct answer as the reward. papers.title: EXAONE 4.0: Unified Large Language Models Integrating Non-reasoning and Reasoning Modes
papers.pitch: A single 32B model, trained with a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that drops PPO and intentionally keeps all-wrong answer groups for richer negative feedback, beats Qwen 3’s 235B model on AIME 2025 (85.3 vs. 72.9) while seamlessly switching between chat and deep reasoning modes. The 1.2B on-device version even tops many mid-size open models on hard math.

papers.pitch: Chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is a brittle mirage: when test problems differ from training data in task structure, length, or format, accuracy collapses from 100% to near zero, even in state-of-the-art models like LLaMA3 and Qwen3. papers.title: Less Is More: Fast and Accurate Reasoning with Cross-Head Unified Sparse Attention
papers.pitch: Existing sparse attention methods cripple reasoning accuracy because small, head-local selection errors snowball across thousands of decoding steps. papers.title: DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning

papers.title: Why Your RL Tuned Reasoning Model Probably Didn’t Learn to Reason: It Just Surfaced What Pre-training Already Planted
papers.pitch: RL post-training creates genuine new reasoning capabilities—but only within a narrow goldilocks zone: when tasks are hard enough that the base model fails, yet close enough to benefit from primitives seeded during pre-training. Outside this boundary, RL either adds nothing or teaches the model to hack the reward without learning to reason.

papers.title: Fantastic Reasoning Behaviors and Where to Find Them: Unsupervised Discovery of the Reasoning Process
papers.pitch: Sparse autoencoders trained on chain-of-thought activations automatically discover 'reasoning vectors' for behaviors like backtracking and reflection—without any human labels—and you can steer them to cut down overthinking while preserving accuracy.

papers.title: On the Optimal Reasoning Length for RL-Trained Language Models
papers.pitch: Length penalties can actively destroy a model’s ability to learn reasoning from scratch, but for models that already know how to reason, the same penalties can make them more efficient—until you push too far and trigger under-thinking.

papers.title: Process Reward Agents for Steering Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning
papers.pitch: Giving frozen language models step-by-step feedback from retrieved medical evidence during generation—rather than after—boosts MedQA accuracy by up to 25.7% and sets a new state of the art at the 4B scale, all without touching the underlying model.

papers.title: AutoTTS: Agentic Discovery for Test-Time Scaling
papers.pitch: Instead of hand-crafting test-time scaling heuristics, this paper shows that an LLM agent can automatically discover superior branching, pruning, and stopping strategies—improving the accuracy–cost Pareto frontier while the entire automated search costs only $39.90 and 160 minutes. papers.title: Reading Wikipedia to Answer Open-Domain Questions
papers.pitch: They built a system that can answer any factoid question directly from raw Wikipedia text, no knowledge base needed — and the retriever is more limiting than the reader: accuracy drops from 70% to under 30% just from moving to open-domain Wikipedia search, despite having state-of-the-art reading comprehension.

papers.title: Latent Retrieval for Weakly Supervised Open Domain Question Answering
papers.pitch: Pre-training a retriever on a made-up ‘Inverse Cloze Task’ lets a QA model learn to find its own evidence across all of Wikipedia using only question-answer pairs—no blackbox IR system needed. On real-world questions where the asker doesn’t already know the answer, this learned retrieval beats BM25 by up to 19 exact-match points.

papers.title: Generalization through Memorization: Nearest Neighbor Language Models
papers.pitch: A standard Transformer LM can achieve state-of-the-art perplexity without any extra training—just by letting it directly copy answers from memorized training examples during inference. papers.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
papers.pitch: Simple dual-encoders fine-tuned only on question–passage pairs smash BM25 retrieval accuracy by up to 19 points—no pretraining tricks needed.

papers.title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
papers.pitch: ColBERT matches the effectiveness of expensive BERT rankers while running 170× faster and using 14,000× fewer FLOPs, by computing query–document similarity through cheap, late interactions between independently pre-computed token-level embeddings. This means you can finally use deep contextualized matching for end-to-end retrieval over millions of passages on a single GPU.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
papers.pitch: A seq2seq model that fetches relevant Wikipedia passages before answering beats all prior systems on open-domain QA—without needing task-specific architectures. When its non-parametric memory is deliberately mismatched (e.g., a 2018 index with a 2020 question), factual accuracy collapses from 70% to 12%, proving that retrieved text, not the generator’s own stored knowledge, drives correctness.

papers.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning for Dense Text Retrieval
papers.pitch: Dense retrieval models lag behind BM25 because in-batch negative sampling produces vanishing gradients and slow convergence. By asynchronously selecting globally hard negatives using the model’s own ANN index during training, ANCE matches the accuracy of a BERT cascade pipeline while being 100× faster.

papers.title: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking
papers.pitch: What if you could have the exact-match precision of BM25 and the semantic fuzziness of dense retrieval inside a single sparse model? papers.title: Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning
papers.pitch: Without any labeled data, a contrastively trained dense retriever beats BM25 on 11 of 15 BEIR benchmarks. This fundamentally challenges the assumption that supervised data is necessary for neural retrieval to work in new domains and languages.

papers.title: Atlas: Few-shot Learning with Retrieval Augmented Language Models
papers.pitch: A mere 11B-parameter model, by retrieving documents, surpasses the few-shot performance of a 540B-parameter model on knowledge tasks—this suggests massive scale is not a prerequisite for few-shot learning when an external memory is available. The key is jointly pre-training the retriever and language model with a novel perplexity distillation loss, teaching the model to read only what it needs.

papers.title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels
papers.pitch: HyDE outperforms fully supervised dense retrievers by generating fake documents from queries—no relevance labels needed. It applies a GPT to hallucinate answers and an encoder to ground those embeddings against real text, filtering fabrication. This language-model-as-generator tactic sees strong gains on web search, QA, and low-resource languages.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Token Retrieval in Multi-Vector Retrieval
papers.pitch: Current multi-vector models bury their most critical information—the document tokens most relevant to the query—in an initial, unoptimized retrieval step, then force an expensive re-scoring over all tokens. papers.title: BM25 Query Augmentation Learned End-to-End
papers.pitch: BM25 accuracy can be nudged higher without any loss of speed by simply appending a learned soft-augmentation mask to its query vector. The trick works so well that it transfers cleanly to unseen datasets, lifting recall by several points with zero extra retrieval cost.

papers.title: Nearest Neighbor Speculative Decoding for LLM Generation and Attribution
papers.pitch: Retrieval-augmented generation can be both high-quality and fast: NEST's relaxed speculative decoding not only accepts chunks of retrieved text to slash inference latency by 1.8× on Llama-2-Chat 70B, but also boosts factual accuracy (FACTSCORE up 21.6%) and provides long, attributable spans covering up to 96% of generated tokens.

papers.title: Scaling Retrieval-Based Language Models with a Trillion-Token Datastore
papers.pitch: Giving a small language model access to a massive 1.4-trillion-token datastore at inference time lets it outperform a model over 10× its size on knowledge tasks, all while costing less to train.

papers.title: Multi-Field Adaptive Retrieval
papers.pitch: MFAR decomposes semi-structured documents into individual fields and scores each independently with both dense and lexical methods, then lets a learned model adaptively weight fields per query—not in advance. This per-query conditioning is crucial: dropping it causes a 16.3% MRR crash, showing that static field weights cannot replace on-the-fly selection.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval
papers.pitch: A single embedding vector cannot realize more than a tiny fraction of possible document rankings—this limit is combinatorial, not circumstantial. Even on a trivial task where queries simply ask 'who likes Apples?', state-of-the-art models fail to retrieve the correct documents, confirming that no amount of scaling can overcome the geometric ceiling of fixed-dimension dense retrieval.

papers.title: Learning to Retrieve from Agent Trajectories
papers.pitch: Search agents don’t use retrieval like humans do—they browse, reject, and reason over documents across multi-turn loops, yet today’s retrievers are still trained on human click data. papers.title: Rethinking Agentic Search with PI-SERINI: Is Lexical Retrieval Sufficient?
papers.pitch: Your expensive dense retriever might be overkill—PI-SERINI hits 83.1% accuracy and 94.7% evidence recall on deep research benchmarks using nothing but tuned BM25 and smart tool-use, outperforming dense-based systems while slashing costs by up to 10×. The secret isn't a fancier retriever but simply giving the agent enough retrieval depth and letting a capable LLM decide when to browse versus read.

papers.title: SparseEmbed: Learning Sparse Lexical Representations with Contextual Embeddings for Retrieval
papers.pitch: Fusing sparse lexical retrieval with contextual embeddings yields a model that beats ColBERTv2 in zero-shot search while staying fast enough for production—each activated token gets its own dense vector, but matching remains linear-time over inverted indexes.

papers.title: Prioritized Experience Replay
papers.pitch: DQN agents learn twice as fast when they ignore boring transitions and focus on their biggest mistakes. papers.title: Asynchronous Methods for Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.pitch: Simply running multiple agents in parallel on a single CPU, without any experience replay, can stabilize deep reinforcement learning across four different algorithms—and the resulting asynchronous actor-critic method (A3C) beats GPU-accelerated DQN on Atari while training in half the time.

papers.title: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
papers.pitch: You can train deep RL agents on complex novel behaviors—like a simulated robot doing a backflip—without a reward function, using under an hour of non-expert human feedback comparing short video clips. papers.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
papers.pitch: PPO matches the reliability of trust-region methods while using only first-order optimization, by simply clipping the policy update so it cannot move too far from the original—a trick that is trivially implemented in a few lines of code yet outperforms far more complex algorithms on continuous control and Atari benchmarks.

papers.title: Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General Reinforcement Learning Algorithm
papers.pitch: A generic reinforcement learning algorithm that starts from random play—knowing nothing but the rules—not only learned superhuman chess in 24 hours but also searches roughly 1,000 times fewer positions per second than the world-champion Stockfish engine, yet still convincingly defeated it.

papers.title: Adaptive Guidance with Reinforcement Meta-Learning
papers.pitch: A recurrent neural network policy learns to land spacecraft on Mars despite random engine failure and on asteroids with unknown gravity—no system identification needed. It even flies blind using raw Doppler radar returns, a task impossible for classical guidance laws.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences

papers.title: Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model

papers.title: Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning

papers.title: Learning to summarize from human feedback
papers.pitch: A 1.3B model fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human preferences outperforms a 10× larger supervised model on summary quality, and the 6.7B version produces summaries preferred over the original human-written demonstrations. This human-feedback approach also transfers to new domains without specific fine-tuning, nearly matching the quality of explicitly trained models.

papers.title: Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling
papers.pitch: Decision Transformer replaces conventional RL algorithms with a GPT-style causal transformer that simply predicts actions from desired returns-to-go and past context. It matches or beats state-of-the-art offline RL methods while naturally handling sparse rewards and long-term credit assignment through self-attention—without dynamic programming, value pessimism, or explicit policy regularization.

papers.title: Secrets of RLHF in Large Language Models: Part I: PPO

The authors show this with a modified loss equation and experimentally validate that loss keeps improving even at 10,0

papers.title: DeepSeek LLM: Scaling Open-Source Language Models with Longtermism
papers.pitch: Scaling laws aren't one-size-fits-all; this paper shows that higher data quality dramatically shifts the optimal balance toward using *much larger models* for the same compute budget, challenging prevailing assumptions. DeepSeek LLM 67B, built with this insight, outperforms LLaMA-2 70B and even beats GPT-3.5 in head-to-head chat evaluations.

papers.title: Gemini 1.5: Unlocking multimodal understanding across millions of tokens of context
papers.pitch: Gemini 1.5 Pro achieves near-perfect recall up to an unprecedented 10 million tokens—an order of magnitude beyond any existing model—and learns to translate a near-extinct language from a single grammar manual as effectively as a human learner. This leap in context length enables processing hours of video or days of audio to unlock surprising in-context learning capabilities, surpassing Gemini 1.0

papers.title: BIMIX: Bivariate Data Mixing Law for Language Model Pretraining
papers.pitch: You can model validation loss as a simple power-law product of a domain’s data proportion and training steps—just 5 coefficients per domain—and then solve directly for the optimal mixture, outperforming expensive data-selection baselines. What’s more, you don’t actually need to train models to set the mixture: entropy-based proxies, especially conditional entropy, already point to the same optimum

papers.title: Scaling Laws with Vocabulary: Larger Models Deserve Larger Vocabularies
papers.pitch: Llama2-70B’s vocabulary is 7× too small for its compute budget, leaving significant performance on the table. Optimal vocabulary size follows a power law where vocabulary parameters grow slower than non-vocabulary parameters, yet most LLMs systematically undershoot this target. Simply replacing the default 32K vocabulary with the predicted optimal 43K vocabulary boosts downstream accuracy by nearl

papers.title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
papers.pitch: Generating hundreds of candidate solutions from weaker LLMs lets them beat state-of-the-art single-shot performance—DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct’s solve rate on SWE-bench Lite jumps from 15.9% to 56%. This coverage scales log-linearly over four orders of magnitude, revealing inference-time scaling laws, but common verification methods plateau without automatic verifiers, leaving untapped potential.

papers.title: Addition Is All You Need for Energy-Efficient Language Models
papers.pitch: Large AI models could run on 95% less energy if we ditch floating-point multipliers and replace them with integer adders—and the math still works. The authors prove that with just 3-bit precision, simple integer addition can match or beat 8-bit floating-point multiplication in transformers with almost no accuracy loss on benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8k.

papers.title: Stuffed Mamba: Oversized States Lead to the Inability to Forget
papers.pitch: Mamba models fail on long contexts not because they forget too much, but because their state size is too large for the training length—allowing them to cheat by retaining everything and bypassing any need to learn forgetting.  Once you train with contexts that exceed the state’s capacity, a 370M Mamba-2 can accurately retrieve a passkey at 256K tokens.

papers.title: Sparsing Law: Towards Large Language Models with Greater Activation Sparsity
papers.pitch: Activation sparsity in LLMs follows convergent power laws with training data, yet the scaling direction flips depending on the activation function—ReLU models get dramatically sparser with more data while SiLU models become denser, converging to a limit insensitive to model scale. By training a 2.4B ReLU model to 93.52% sparsity, the authors achieve a 4.1× inference speedup with only 1% perplexity

papers.title: Densing Law of LLMs
papers.pitch: The effective compute needed to match frontier LLM performance halves every ~3.3 months—LLM capability density is doubling exponentially, not scaling up. This means a model with half the parameters can rival the previous state-of-the-art roughly every quarter, compressing decades of hardware gains into mere months and fundamentally rewriting the economics of deployment.

papers.title: LongRoPE2: Near-Lossless LLM Context Window Scaling
papers.pitch: Extending an LLM’s context window usually kills its original short-range abilities—but LongRoPE2 recovers over 98.5% of them while reaching 128K tokens, using just 10B training tokens. The trick is pinpointing which RoPE dimensions are critically undertrained and fixing only those, with a needle-in-a-haystack perplexity probe that picks the golden rescaling factors.

papers.title: Inference-Time Scaling for Generalist Reward Modeling
papers.pitch: A generative reward model trained with self-generated principles, given 32× more inference compute, can outperform a 671B MoE model at reward evaluation—but only on tasks within its generalist range, while scalar reward models still dominate verifiable reasoning. The method introduces Self-Principled Critique Tuning (SPCT) via online RL and a meta reward model to filter sampled critiques, pushing

papers.title: Parallel Scaling Law for Language Models
papers.pitch: A model using multiple parallel forward passes can match the performance of a nearly twice-as-large single-pass model while increasing memory by up to 22× less and latency by 6× less, fundamentally redefining the cost of scaling intelligence.

papers.title: Fast and Simplex: 2-Simplicial Attention in Triton
papers.pitch: Unlike standard Transformer modifications that merely shift error curves, replacing dot-product attention with a trilinear 2-simplicial form steepens the scaling exponent—loss drops faster as parameters grow on math and reasoning tasks. This 18–20% boost in scaling slope challenges the long-held belief that architectural changes cannot change the fundamental power-law exponent, while a practical T

papers.title: Scaling Laws Meet Model Architecture: Toward Inference-Efficient LLMs
papers.pitch: For a fixed parameter and training token budget, simply tweaking hidden size and MLP-to-attention ratio yields models that are both 2.1% more accurate and 42% faster at inference than LLaMA-3.2. The key is a conditional scaling law that predicts how these architectural choices shift the loss curve, enabling a direct search for Pareto-optimal designs without guesswork.

papers.title: Scaling Search Relevance: Augmenting App Store Ranking with LLM-Generated Judgments
papers.pitch: A fine-tuned 3B-parameter model crushes a 30B pretrained one at generating textual relevance labels, achieving an F1 of 0.800 versus 0.382. papers.title: Train-to-Test (T2) Scaling Laws: Integrating Pretraining and Test-Time Compute
papers.pitch: When you account for the cost of repeated sampling at inference, the optimal pretraining recipe flips: you should train much smaller models on vastly more data than Chinchilla recommends. These deliberately overtrained models beat Chinchilla-optimal ones by a wide margin across all tasks, and the advantage remarkably survives fine-tuning.

papers.title: Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction by Locally Linear Embedding
papers.pitch: You can recover the global shape of a twisted manifold buried in high-dimensional space using only the simplest possible local ingredient: how to reconstruct each point from its immediate neighbors. This method requires no distance measurements between distant points and avoids the local minima that plague other nonlinear techniques, solving a single sparse eigenproblem instead.

papers.title: Local structures of gravity-free space and time and their phenomena
papers.pitch: Special relativity's assumption of a flat, pseudo-Euclidean local spacetime may be an oversimplification—this paper proposes that gravity-free space and time inherently possess a generalized Finslerian geometry, offering a structural revision that preserves the constancy of light speed and local Lorentz invariance while potentially reconciling the theory with quantum and statistical mechanics.

papers.title: Spanner: Google’s Globally-Distributed Database
papers.pitch: Spanner achieves externally consistent transactions at global scale by exposing clock uncertainty as a first-class API, using atomic clocks and GPS to bound time errors to under 10 ms. This lets the system enforce real-time commit ordering across continents with only a ~5 ms penalty, breaking the long-held assumption that globally synchronous replication is prohibitively slow.

papers.title: Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data
papers.pitch: Relationships between entities can be modeled as simple vector translations (h + ℓ ≈ t) in embedding space, achieving state-of-the-art link prediction with far fewer parameters. This surprisingly simple approach, TransE, outperforms more complex bilinear and tensor factorization models on large knowledge bases like Freebase, proving that a basic translation assumption is enough to capture complex

papers.title: Clipper: A Low-Latency Online Prediction Serving System
papers.pitch: Clipper sits between applications and ML frameworks, using adaptive batching and multi-armed bandit model selection to slash prediction latency while boosting throughput and accuracy—without touching the models themselves. Surprisingly, its modular, container-based design matches TensorFlow Serving on throughput and latency, but adds straggler mitigation and real-time model composition for free.

papers.title: TensorFlow-Serving: Flexible, High-Performance ML Serving
papers.pitch: Naive production ML serving quickly collapses under versioning, hardware acceleration, and model-bloat demands—a trap that snared most teams at Google. This paper shows how TensorFlow-Serving’s modular, latency-optimized architecture avoids those pitfalls, sustaining ~100K requests per second per core and scaling to tens of millions of inferences per second across Google’s production fleet.

papers.title: DeepSpeed Inference: Enabling Efficient Inference of Transformer Models at Unprecedented Scale
papers.pitch: DeepSpeed Inference serves a trillion-parameter model in under 25ms by exploiting over 100 TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth across hundreds of GPUs. It also runs models 25× larger than GPU memory on a single commodity workstation at over 50% of peak throughput.

papers.title: EFFICIENTLY SCALING TRANSFORMER INFERENCE
papers.pitch: Even a 540B-parameter model can deliver a token in 29ms and process kilometer-long contexts—if you abandon head-parallel strategies in favor of batch-sharded multiquery attention. The same model hits 76% peak utilization during large-batch prefill by dynamically switching between weight-stationary and weight-gathered layouts based on whether the workload is decode-bound or prefill-bound.

papers.title: AlpaServe: Statistical Multiplexing with Model Parallelism for Deep Learning Serving
papers.pitch: Even when a model fits on one GPU, deliberately splitting it across multiple GPUs—increasing per-request latency—can slash overall response times under bursty traffic by pooling resources across models. papers.title: Fast Distributed Inference Serving for Large Language Models
papers.pitch: FastServe demonstrates that GPU memory overflow, not scheduling granularity, is the hidden bottleneck in token-level preemptive scheduling for LLM inference—addressing it via proactive KV cache offloading yields up to 31.4× throughput gains over vLLM under identical latency targets.

papers.title: SpecInfer: Accelerating Large Language Model Serving with Tree-based Speculative Inference and Verification
papers.pitch: SpecInfer turns the standard sequential token generation of large language models on its head by verifying entire trees of candidate tokens in a single forward pass, boosting serving speed by up to 3.5× without altering model quality. papers.title:
Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with
  PagedAttention
papers.pitch: Current LLM serving systems waste up to 96% of GPU memory on KV cache fragmentation, massively limiting batch sizes. PagedAttention eliminates this waste by treating the KV cache like virtual memory—splitting it into blocks that can be mapped non-contiguously—and vLLM, the system built on it, delivers 2–4× higher throughput without latency penalties.

papers.title: PUNICA: MULTI-TENANT LORA SERVING
papers.pitch: Serving hundreds of distinct LoRA models on a shared GPU achieves the same throughput as serving a single model. Punica collapses multi-tenant workloads onto minimal GPUs using a novel kernel that batches different LoRA computations against one copy of the base model, yielding a 12× throughput gain with negligible latency overhead.

papers.title: ATOM: Low-Bit Quantization for Efficient and Accurate LLM Serving
papers.pitch: While modern GPUs pack INT4 tensor cores with 4× the throughput of FP16, prior quantization methods either left this performance on the table or suffered severe accuracy crashes—Atom unlocks a 7.73× end-to-end throughput gain over FP16 by keeping just 128 outlier channels at higher precision and fusing dequantization directly into the GEMM pipeline, all at negligible accuracy loss.

papers.title: Relax: Composable Abstractions for End-to-End Dynamic Machine Learning
papers.pitch: Existing ML compilers struggle to optimize dynamic-shape models across diverse hardware, but Relax matches or beats hand-tuned systems on GPUs while also enabling deployment to mobile and web browsers that those systems don't support. papers.title: S-LORA: SERVING THOUSANDS OF CONCURRENT LORA ADAPTERS

papers.title: ZeroQuant(4+2): Redefining LLMs Quantization with a New FP6-Centric Strategy for Diverse Generative Tasks
papers.pitch: Even large 13B+ models suffer severe quality drops on code generation and summarization with standard INT4 quantization. Shifting to FP6—long dismissed as impractical—matches FP16 accuracy on these same tasks, and a new 4+2 kernel design makes it as fast as fine-grained INT4, offering a drop-in solution where INT4 fails.

papers.title: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving
papers.pitch: Colocating prefill and decoding on the same GPU drags down LLM serving throughput—DistServe breaks them apart to serve up to 7.4× more requests within tight latency SLOs. By assigning each phase to dedicated hardware and co-optimizing its resource plan, the system sidesteps the prefill-decoding interference that forces existing servers to over-provision or miss targets.

papers.title: FP6-LLM: Efficiently Serving Large Language Models Through FP6-Centric Algorithm-System Co-Design

papers.title: Hydragen: High-Throughput LLM Inference with Shared Prefixes

papers.title: FIDDLER: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.pitch: Large Mixture-of-Experts models barely fit in GPU memory, yet simply offloading layers to CPU kills performance. Fiddler shows that by dynamically routing sparse expert computations to CPU or GPU based on token load—exploiting CPU’s near-linear latency scaling and GPU’s weight-transfer overheads—it outperforms all existing systems across every inference scenario, achieving up to an 11.57× speedup

papers.title: Inference Performance Optimization for Large Language Models on CPUs

Their SlimAttention further outperforms FlashAttention on CPU by 10× at 256 tokens, making CPU deployment genuinely practical for the first time.

papers.title: LiNR: Model Based Neural Retrieval on GPUs at LinkedIn
papers.pitch: LinkedIn’s LiNR replaces traditional ANN indexes with a fully differentiable GPU model, collapsing retrieval and ranking into a single forward pass—and proves the payoff with a 3% lift in professional daily active users.

papers.title: NanoFlow: Towards Optimal Large Language Model Serving Throughput
papers.pitch: Contrary to conventional wisdom that LLM serving is memory-bound, NanoFlow reveals it is actually compute-bound—yet existing systems waste over 60% of GPU compute by running sequential operations. NanoFlow reclaims lost throughput by overlapping compute, memory, and networking via fine-grained nano-batching, delivering a 1.91× speedup and hitting 50–72% of theoretical peak.

papers.title: Is the GPU Half-Empty or Half-Full? Practical Scheduling Techniques for LLMs
papers.pitch: A 20-line scheduler that prioritizes small requests under load can cut time-to-first-token latency in half compared to state-of-the-art alternatives, without the complexity of prediction-based methods. Meanwhile, a simple token-aware load balancer outperforms general-purpose policies just by estimating queue wait times from available memory.

papers.title: ThunderKittens: Simple, Fast, and Adorable AI Kernels

papers.title: ShadowKV: KV Cache in Shadows for High-Throughput Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.pitch: ShadowKV achieves up to 3× throughput gains on long-context LLM inference by compressing the KV cache—but the crucial twist is that it compresses keys *before* rotary position encoding, exploiting a previously overlooked low-rank property of pre-RoPE representations that enables 6× compression without accuracy loss while value caches are simply offloaded to CPU.

papers.title: MARCONI: PREFIX CACHING FOR THE ERA OF HYBRID LLMS
papers.pitch: Hybrid LLMs combining attention with recurrent layers break prefix caching because their in-place state updates cannot be rolled back—forcing a choice between caching huge, rarely-reused checkpoints or forgoing reuse. Marconi recovers up to 34.4× higher token hit rates by rejecting cache entries that are unlikely to be reused and evicting based on FLOP savings per byte instead of recency.

papers.title: Efficiently Serving LLM Reasoning Programs with Certaindex
papers.pitch: LLM reasoning often wastes 3× more tokens than needed because models keep generating long after their answers stabilize. The authors show that a lightweight metric—Certaindex—can detect this settling point and trigger early exit, cutting compute by up to 50% without hurting accuracy and boosting serving throughput by 3.3×.

papers.pitch: A 10× throughput boost—achieved by pruning the model 40%, summarizing items with a specialized RL agent, and stripping out autoregressive generation—makes LLM-based ranking viable at millions of requests per second. Naive content compression actually hurts more than it helps, but aligning the summarizer to the ranker preserves quality within 2%.

papers.title: RDMA Point-to-Point Communication for LLM Systems

papers.title: DualPath: Breaking the Storage Bandwidth Bottleneck in Agentic LLM Inference
papers.pitch: In agentic LLM serving, up to 99% of each request’s context comes from cache—turning inference into a massive storage I/O problem where prefill engines are starved for bandwidth while decode engines sit idle. DualPath shatters this bottleneck by routing KV-cache loads through decode engines first, then RDMA-transferring them to prefill, boosting throughput up to 1.96×.

papers.title: Accelerating t-SNE using Tree-Based Algorithms

papers.title: High-Performance Distributed ML at Scale through Parameter Server Consistency Models
papers.pitch: ML algorithms converge faster not by enforcing perfect parameter consistency, but by bounding how much in-flight parameter updates differ across workers—a theoretical insight that leads to an eager communication strategy, cutting staleness by pushing updates aggressively rather than waiting for pull requests.

papers.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

papers.title: Delving Deep into Rectifiers: Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification

Stochastic binarization acts as a regularizer, improving test accuracy on CIFAR-10 to 8.27% without data augmentation, while eliminating most multiplications and enabling up to 16× memory reduction at test time.

papers.title: Layer Normalization
papers.pitch: What if we could normalize neural networks across features instead of across data samples—making training faster without depending on batch size? Layer normalization shows that computing statistics within a single layer on a single training case stabilizes hidden state dynamics in RNNs far better than batch normalization, cutting convergence time by up to 40% while improving generalization.

papers.title: Wasserstein GAN
papers.pitch: Standard GANs fail because their Jensen-Shannon loss yields zero gradient when real and generated distributions lie on disjoint low-dimensional manifolds—the exact case for images. By switching to the Earth-Mover distance, WGANs provide a meaningful, continuous critic loss that correlates with sample quality and eliminates the vanishing gradient problem.

papers.title: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning for Fast Adaptation of Deep Networks
papers.pitch: Instead of learning an update rule or relying on special architectures, this paper shows you can simply *train the initial parameters* of any model to be exquisitely sensitive to a few gradient steps on new data. This one trick produces state-of-the-art few-shot classification and lets reinforcement learning agents adapt to new goals with just two gradient updates, making meta-learning compatible

papers.title: Mixed Precision Training
papers.pitch: Training massive neural networks in half-precision (FP16) halves memory and doubles speed without losing accuracy—as long as you keep a single-precision master copy of the weights, scale the loss to preserve tiny gradients, and accumulate dot products in FP32.

papers.title: mixup: Beyond Empirical Risk Minimization
papers.pitch: Training on random convex combinations of input pairs and their labels—so-called mixup—forces networks to behave linearly between examples. This embarrassingly simple trick dramatically boosts robustness to label noise and adversarial attacks while simultaneously improving clean accuracy on ImageNet and CIFAR.

papers.title: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization
papers.pitch: L2 regularization and weight decay are not equivalent in Adam—standard implementations apply L2 regularization, which inadvertently penalizes large-gradient parameters less than small-gradient ones, explaining much of Adam’s generalization gap relative to SGD. By simply decoupling the weight decay step from the adaptive gradient update (forming AdamW), the authors close this gap on CIFAR-10 by 15%

papers.title: Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification
papers.pitch: Fine-tuning language models for NLP tasks was thought to require millions of in‑domain documents—until ULMFiT showed that three simple training tricks let an LSTM match the performance of training from scratch using 100× less labeled data.

papers.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks
papers.pitch: A randomly initialized neural network already contains a tiny subnetwork that can train in isolation to match the full model’s accuracy—sometimes even faster—but the catch is you must reuse the original initial weights, not reinitialize randomly. Pruning alone isn’t enough; the specific initialization values are the real "winning ticket."

papers.title: Mesh-TensorFlow: Deep Learning for Supercomputers
papers.pitch: Mesh-TensorFlow lets you scale Transformers to 5 billion parameters—not by just splitting the batch, but by sharding any tensor dimension across a multidimensional processor grid. This approach hits state-of-the-art translation and language modeling results while keeping over 50% hardware efficiency on 512 TPU cores, where pure data-parallelism would simply run out of memory.

papers.title: Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning without Exploration
papers.pitch: Standard off-policy deep RL algorithms like DDPG can completely fail to learn anything from a fixed dataset—performing even worse than the behavioral policy that collected it—due to a newly identified extrapolation error in value estimation. The proposed Batch-Constrained deep Q-learning (BCQ) overcomes this by forcing the policy to choose only actions grounded in the data, enabling the first cont

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP
papers.pitch: Adapter modules added to a frozen BERT model match full fine-tuning performance on GLUE—within 0.4%—while training only 3.6% of the parameters per task. This near-identity initialization trick makes tiny bottleneck layers work, offering a two-orders-of-magnitude parameter reduction with no loss in accuracy. The method enables a single extensible model to handle a stream of tasks without catastroph

papers.title: An Effective Approach to Unsupervised Machine Translation
papers.pitch: Unsupervised translation leapfrogs a supervised champion: By fixing broken subword scoring in SMT and then switching to NMT, a system with zero parallel data achieves 22.5 BLEU on English–German WMT 2014—0.5 points higher than the best *supervised* entry from that year.

papers.title: Adaptive Attention Span in Transformers
papers.pitch: Transformer self-attention heads naturally learn vastly different optimal context sizes — some attend only to the most recent 32 tokens while others span thousands of steps. By letting each head dynamically mask its own attention span via a learned soft mask, we can extend the maximum context to over 8,000 tokens with no loss in accuracy, while slashing inference FLOPS by up to 70%.

papers.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
papers.pitch: You don't actually need separate architectures or objectives for different NLP tasks—casting everything from translation to classification into a simple text-to-text format with task prefixes works state-of-the-art. A massive empirical study reveals that a denoising objective that randomly replaces token spans with a single sentinel outperforms all prior pre-training strategies, including BERT-sty

papers.title: BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training for Natural Language Generation, Translation, and Comprehension
papers.pitch: BART smashes the wall between understanding and generation models: a single pretrained denoising autoencoder matches RoBERTa on comprehension tasks while absolutely crushing prior art on text generation—for instance, a 6 ROUGE leap on abstractive summarization. The secret is training a standard Transformer to reconstruct text that was corrupted by both sentence shuffling and a novel span-infilling

papers.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers.pitch: You don’t need a separate distillation loss to train a smaller BERT—just gradually swap its layers for compact ones during fine-tuning. This progressive module replacement, inspired by the Ship of Theseus paradox, lets the remaining original layers dynamically adapt to the new modules, matching or beating standard knowledge distillation while using only the task loss.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Survey
papers.pitch: Matching intermediate-layer feature activations or instance relationships between teacher and student models yields significantly better compression than only copying the teacher's final softened outputs. Knowledge distillation reduces model size while paradoxically delivering 0.5–8 percentage point accuracy gains over training the student from scratch. Yet this powerful transfer often breaks down

papers.title: Modifying Memories in Transformer Models
papers.pitch: You can surgically edit facts inside a Transformer without retraining from scratch—but counterintuitively, limiting weight updates to the first or last layers works better than fine-tuning the entire model. This constrained, layer-specific approach lets language models forget outdated knowledge and learn new facts while leaving the rest of their memory intact.

papers.title: Making Pre-trained Language Models Better Few-shot Learners
papers.pitch: Fine-tuning a moderate-sized language model like RoBERTa-large on just 32 training examples can hit ~90% accuracy on most binary NLP benchmarks, matching GPT-3’s few-shot performance without the 175B-parameter cost. The key is automatically finding the right prompt templates and label words—no human guesswork needed—and then dynamically inserting similar examples into the prompt itself.

papers.title: Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation
papers.pitch: By learning just 0.1% of a language model's parameters—a small set of continuous vectors prepended to the input—prefix-tuning matches full fine-tuning performance on generation tasks and actually outperforms it when training data is scarce. This modular approach eliminates the need to store a full model copy per task, making large-scale personalized deployment practical.

papers.title: ZeRO-Offload: Democratizing Billion-Scale Model Training
papers.pitch: A single GPU can now train a 13-billion-parameter model—10× larger than PyTorch’s limit—and still run 40 TFLOPS, exceeding the speed of much smaller in-memory baselines. ZeRO-Offload achieves this through a unique partitioning that offloads only optimizer states and gradients to CPU compute, hitting the theoretical minimum data movement.

papers.title: The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning
papers.pitch: Prompt tuning, which prepends a handful of learned virtual tokens to the input of a frozen language model, can match the performance of full model fine-tuning—but only once the underlying model exceeds billions of parameters. This finding overturns the assumption that lightweight adaptation methods inherently sacrifice quality, revealing a scaling law where task-specific competence emerges in the

papers.title: Contrastive Learning for Many-to-many Multilingual Neural Machine Translation
papers.pitch: A multilingual translation model trained only on English-centric parallel data can leap from near-zero to over 15 BLEU on unseen non-English pairs like German→French simply by pulling aligned sentence representations closer and pushing random ones apart. This contrastive trick, combined with smart dictionary-based data noising, unlocks many-to-many translation without ever showing the model a non-

papers.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.pitch: Freezing a 175B-parameter model and only training tiny rank-decomposition matrices injected into each layer matches full fine-tuning—while cutting trainable parameters 10,000×, reducing GPU memory use by 3×, and adding zero inference latency. Even a rank of 1 or 2 suffices to capture the necessary task-specific weight updates, suggesting the learned adaptations are intrinsically low-dimensional.

papers.title: BitFit: Simple Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning for Transformer-based Masked Language-models
papers.pitch: You can match full BERT fine-tuning performance across GLUE tasks by adjusting just the bias terms—a mere 0.09% of all parameters—and halving that to 0.04% loses almost nothing. This exposes that fine-tuning is mainly about steering pre-existing knowledge, not learning new rules, and makes deploying one backbone for hundreds of tasks lightweight enough to be practical.

papers.title: Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners
papers.pitch: Fine-tuning a 137B model solely on task instructions—without examples—enables it to outperform zero-shot GPT-3 on 20 of 25 unseen benchmarks and even beat few-shot GPT-3 on several reasoning tasks. This “instruction tuning” transforms a standard language model into a zero-shot powerhouse, but only when the base model exceeds 8B parameters; smaller models collapse under the same process.

papers.title: Recursively Summarizing Books with Human Feedback
papers.pitch: We trained GPT-3 to summarize entire books by decomposing them into small, human-evaluable chunks and recursively summarizing the summaries — all without requiring labelers to read the full 500-page novels. The resulting model produces plausible book-length summaries that in 5% of cases rival human quality, while cutting supervision costs by over 50× compared to an end-to-end approach.

papers.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
papers.pitch: Neural networks can suddenly jump from chance-level to perfect generalization long after they’ve perfectly memorized the training data — a phenomenon the authors call “grokking.” Weight decay is the secret sauce that makes it happen, not early stopping or dropout.

papers.title: BLOOM: A 176B-Parameter Open-Access Multilingual Language Model
papers.pitch: Training a 176B-parameter multilingual model on 46 languages actually produced competitive NLP performance—matching proprietary giants—while emitting only 25 tons of CO₂, roughly a third of comparable efforts. But the paper’s starkest finding is that for truly low-resource languages like Swahili↔Yoruba, the model completely collapses to near-zero translation quality, demonstrating that scale alone

papers.title: The Flan Collection: Designing Data and Methods for Effective Instruction Tuning
papers.pitch: Mixing zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompts during instruction tuning—counterintuitively—improves performance in *all* modes, and simply adding 10% few-shot examples boosts zero-shot results by over 2%. This paper also reveals that task-balancing and data enrichment, not just scale, are the hidden keys to unlocking models that converge faster and higher on downstream tasks.

papers.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
papers.pitch: A 6.7B-parameter model that teaches itself to call calculators, search engines, and QA systems outperforms 175B GPT-3 on zero-shot tasks—without a single human annotation telling it when tools are useful.

papers.title: LLaMA-Adapter: Efficient Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models with Zero-Initialized Attention
papers.pitch: LLaMA-Adapter freezes the entire 7B-parameter LLaMA model and adds just 1.2M new parameters – a gating factor initialized to zero – yet matches the instruction-following performance of fully fine-tuned Alpaca while training 3× faster. The same zero-initialized attention trick seamlessly extends the frozen language model to multi-modal reasoning without catastrophic forgetting, achieving top result

papers.title: Instruction Tuning with GPT-4
papers.pitch: A 7B open-source LLaMA model, fine-tuned solely on GPT-4-generated examples, nearly matches the instruction-following prowess of GPT-4 itself—winning 54% of head-to-head helpfulness comparisons against a GPT-3.5-trained counterpart. The secret lies in distilling the stronger teacher’s output, which yields superior alignment even at a fraction of the size.

papers.title: QLORA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
papers.pitch: QLORA slashes the memory needed to fine-tune a 65B model from over 780GB to under 48GB—fitting on a single consumer GPU—with zero performance loss versus full 16-bit training. papers.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
papers.pitch: You can now fine-tune a 30B-parameter language model on a single GPU using only forward passes, matching backpropagation’s performance while consuming just the memory of inference. papers.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
papers.pitch: You can align language models with human preferences using a simple classification loss—no reward modeling, no reinforcement learning, and no sampling from the policy during training. papers.title: Faster Causal Attention Over Large Sequences Through Sparse Flash Attention
papers.pitch: Sparse attention can be dramatically faster than dense FlashAttention—if you stop treating the causal mask as a rigid triangle. By extending FlashAttention to handle dynamic, block-wise sparsity patterns like hashing and query/key dropping, the authors achieve up to 3.3× training speedups on sequences of 16k tokens with no perplexity loss.

papers.title: Orca: Progressive Learning from Complex Explanation Traces of GPT-4
papers.pitch: A 13B model can match ChatGPT's reasoning by learning its step-by-step thought process—not just its answers. Orca surpasses Vicuna-13B by over 100% on complex reasoning benchmarks simply by being trained on GPT-4's detailed explanations, proving that small models are limited by shallow imitation signals, not by scale.

papers.title: Full Parameter Fine-tuning for Large Language Models with Limited Resources
papers.pitch: You can fine‑tune a full 65B model on a single 8×RTX 3090 machine, matching the quality of distributed training—by fusing backward pass and parameter updates so that the only gradient stored is the one flowing through the current layer.

papers.title: Training Transformers with 4-bit Integers
papers.pitch: You can train transformers entirely in INT4 on current GPUs and get up to 35% speedup over FP16—provided you tame activation outliers with a Hadamard transform and approximate backprop gradients via bit splitting and importance sampling. This work finally makes 4-bit training practical on off-the-shelf hardware.

papers.pitch: Training a student language model on its own self-generated outputs rather than on a fixed dataset can double distillation gains, slashing the performance gap to the teacher. This simple on-policy approach not only fixes the train–inference mismatch but also unlocks flexible divergences and seamless integration with RL fine-tuning—without needing a separate data generation phase.

papers.title: Scaling Relationship on Learning Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models
papers.pitch: Pre-training loss, not model size, is the real driver of math reasoning ability—and when you let LLMs teach themselves via rejection sampling, the weakest models gain the most, because what matters isn't just more data but more *distinct reasoning paths*.

papers.title: RETROFORMER: RETROSPECTIVE LARGE LANGUAGE AGENTS WITH POLICY GRADIENT OPTIMIZATION
papers.pitch: LLM agents can learn from their mistakes without ever touching the giant model’s weights—just by training a 7B-parameter critic to write better post-mortem reflections. This turns self-reflection into a proper policy gradient problem, letting the agent pinpoint *why* it failed and fix it faster, boosting success rates by up to 15% on embodied tasks over frozen verbal feedback alone.

papers.title: Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions
papers.pitch: Large language models fail to recognize key information when the order of phrases is simply reversed, with influence dropping to near-zero—revealing a fundamental brittleness beneath their seemingly sophisticated reasoning. papers.title: YARN: EFFICIENT CONTEXT WINDOW EXTENSION OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
papers.pitch: Need 10x less data to double a model’s context window? YaRN achieves this by sparing high-frequency RoPE dimensions from interpolation and calming attention logits, extending LLaMA to 128k tokens while nearly preserving short-context accuracy with just 400 training steps.

papers.title: LoftQ: LoRA-Fine-Tuning-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.pitch: Standard quantization causes catastrophic LoRA fine-tuning failure at 2-bit, but LoftQ enables convergence and even outperforms the full-precision model at that extreme compression level. The method jointly optimizes the quantized backbone and its low-rank adapters to start from a point that faithfully approximates the original weights.

papers.title: VeRA: Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation
papers.pitch: VeRA slashes LoRA’s trainable parameters by up to 100× without losing performance—by freezing a single random low-rank matrix pair in amber across all layers and learning only tiny scaling vectors. This means you no longer have to store a unique, massive adapter for every user or task, just a handful of scalars that modulate the same fixed random projections.

papers.title: FP8-LM: Training FP8 Large Language Models
papers.pitch: Training 175B-parameter GPT models with FP8 data formats runs 75% faster than standard BF16 approaches and slashes memory by 39%—without any loss in accuracy. papers.title: Camels in a Changing Climate: Enhancing LM Adaptation with Tulu 2

papers.title: Self-Play Fine-Tuning Converts Weak Language Models to Strong Language Models
papers.pitch: A weak LLM can bootstrap itself into a stronger one without any extra human data simply by playing against its own earlier, less-refined outputs—treating the model's own past generations as negative examples. papers.title: Tuning Language Models by Proxy

papers.title: WARM: On the Benefits of Weight Averaged Reward Models
papers.pitch: Weight averaging reward models—rather than ensembling their predictions—acts as a regularizer that suppresses memorized, brittle features, dramatically improving robustness to distribution shift and label noise during RLHF. A policy fine-tuned with this method achieves a 79.4% win rate against one trained with a single reward model.

papers.title: The Hedgehog & the Porcupine: Expressive Linear Attentions with Softmax Mimicry
papers.pitch: Linear attentions can match softmax attention—often perfectly—if you simply train them to mimic its spiky, monotonic weight distributions. Hedgehog does exactly this, recovering over 99% of BERT’s GLUE score and turning pretrained GPT‑2 and Llama‑2 7B into competitive sub‑quadratic models without any extra attention modules.

papers.title: Resonance RoPE: Improving Context Length Generalization of Large Language Models
papers.pitch: Standard RoPE extrapolation methods fail because nearly half of a model’s positional features are *interpolated* rather than extrapolated when handling unseen long contexts. Resonance RoPE eliminates this gap by snapping each feature’s wavelength to an integer, instantly correcting faulty position recognition without any runtime overhead or retraining.

papers.title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
papers.pitch: You can pre-train a 7B-parameter LLM on a single consumer GPU with just 24 GB of memory—no model parallelism or offloading needed. GaLore achieves this by showing that gradient matrices are naturally low-rank during training, so compressing the optimizer states via gradient projection cuts memory use by up to 82.5% without sacrificing performance compared to full-rank baselines.

papers.title: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG

papers.title: InternLM2 Technical Report

papers.title: ChatGLM-Math: Improving Math Problem-Solving in Large Language Models with a Self-Critique Pipeline

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.pitch: Forget tweaking millions of weights—LoReFT fine-tunes language models by editing hidden representations in a low-rank subspace, matching or beating state-of-the-art PEFTs while using 15×–65× fewer parameters than LoRA. The method scales especially well with larger models, suggesting that steering representations directly is a more efficient path to adaptation than classical weight updates.

papers.title: Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language
papers.pitch: Language models trained only on correct answers never learn to backtrack—but when shown messy, mistake-filled search traces for a math puzzle, they solve 25% more problems. papers.title: MiniCPM: Unveiling the Potential of Small Language Models with Scalable Training Strategies
papers.pitch: Small 1–2B models can rival 7B–13B models when trained with a new learning rate scheduler that reveals the optimal data-to-model ratio is nearly 10× larger than previously believed. The key innovation lets researchers study scaling laws without retraining from scratch, slashing the cost of finding optimal model sizes.

papers.title: Learn Your Reference Model for Real Good Alignment

This simple change makes offline methods competitive with online RLHF without reward model hacking.

papers.title: Iterative Reasoning Preference Optimization
papers.pitch: Standard iterative preference optimization fails on reasoning tasks, but adding a negative log-likelihood (NLL) term to DPO—so the model is also trained to directly maximize the probability of correct answers—reverses this, boosting GSM8K accuracy from 55.6% to 81.6% on Llama-2-70B-Chat by iteratively preferring winning over losing chain-of-thought steps.

papers.title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction
papers.pitch: Training language models to guess the next *four* words at once—not just one—makes 13B-parameter models solve 12–17% more programming problems, with zero extra training cost. The technique forces models to plan ahead, building better reasoning circuits, and triples inference speed.

papers.title: RLHF Workflow: From Reward Modeling to Online RLHF
papers.pitch: Open-source 8B models trained with online iterative RLHF can beat GPT-3.5-turbo and match 70B models on chat benchmarks—without relying on any proprietary data or human labelers.
